title: In 74 epilepsy patients, same-session spontaneous ECoG coupling predicted stimulation-evoked N1 responses beyond distance and electrode effects, but its direction did not predict response direction
abstract: Question: inside one patient and session, does spontaneous coupling between ECoG electrodes predict causal single-pulse stimulation responses (CCEP N1) after distance and electrode identity are removed, and does the direction of spontaneous coupling predict the response direction? Data: OpenNeuro ds004080 v1.2.4 (CC0), 74 patients aged 4-51; the authors' N1 detections; 60 s (two patients 120 s) of clean spontaneous ECoG per patient from the same run, read with HTTP range requests (pre-stimulation rest, inter-train gaps, then 3.0-4.8 s inter-pulse windows with the stimulus-locked mean removed). Measures: broadband correlation, band amplitude-envelope correlation (AEC), orthogonalised AEC, coherence and imaginary coherence; phase-slope index and lagged high-gamma envelope asymmetry for direction. Method: as in sci:sha256:8811ade9, within-patient 5-fold cross-validated logistic models of N1 presence with a distance spline and one fixed effect per stimulated pair and recording electrode (241,384 edges, 31,869 N1); 20 surrogates per patient that permute coupling inside 5 mm distance bins; a 20 mm or more robustness run; for direction, a Bradley-Terry model with electrode send/receive parameters (23,991 asymmetric pairs, 72 patients). Results: coupling reduced held-out log-loss by 18.4 millibits per edge (95% CI 14.2-23.0; 86% of patients positive), against -7.0 for shuffles and 0.93 for group tractography in the earlier study; leakage-robust measures alone gave 10.3 (7.6-13.1); at 20 mm or more the gain was 21.4 (16.7-26.4). Broadband and 4-30 Hz envelope coupling carried more than high-gamma. The gain was about 38% of that from electrode identity. Direction failed: sign agreement 0.50-0.51 for all directed measures, no gain over the electrode model, electrode-level rho 0.00-0.03. Limitations: one centre, automatic N1 detection, short spontaneous segments (gains are probably lower bounds), common-average reference, tractography compared on a different edge set.

citations.reason: Same within-patient CCEP model design; its group-tractography gain (0.93 mbit) is the comparison point.
Electrode send/receive balance sets most CCEP asymmetry; our direction test confirms that pair-level spontaneous direction adds nothing.

Interictal iEEG coupling against tractography in another cohort; here coupling is compared with causal responses.
Spontaneous lag direction did not follow axon direction in mouse; here it does not follow causal stimulation direction in human ECoG.
Pair-specific anatomical wiring added almost nothing to FC; contrast with the large functional-to-causal match here.
Individual connectomes predict individual FC better than group ones; consistent with the individual advantage here.
